title: Do Miracles Really Happen?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Carlos Eire arrived in Miami at age 11 in 1962, a refugee from Castro’s Cuba
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Carlos Eire arrived in Miami at age 11 in 1962, a refugee from Castro’s Cuba
Three years passed before his mother could join him, and he never saw his father again
This experience of dislocation profoundly shaped Eire’s work as a religious historian
In his latest book, They Flew , Eire looks at early modern reports of miracles

Drawing on his own experience of moving between cultures and worldviews, he tries to imagine himself into the minds of those who claimed to have witnessed levitations, bilocations, and other impossible occurrences, and he asks what we can learn by taking these reports seriously
David Brooks talks with Eire about magic, empathy, and the past as a foreign country
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: This is a conversation about radical empathy
We live in a polarized age, often with people whose modes of consciousness are utterly alien to our own

We hear someone spew a conspiracy theory or utter an opinion that seems monstrous, and we think: How on earth can they think that way? But being a good citizen in this sort of pluralistic society requires that kind of radical empathy
It means approaching those who are different with a willingness and an ability to stand in their standpoint, to enter into, at least a little, how they see the world
My guest is Carlos Eire, who has been trained by life to excel at this
When he was a boy, he was airlifted out of Cuba by parents who wanted to get him away from Castro’s revolution
He worked his way through college, got a Ph.D. here at Yale, where he is now a professor of history and religious studies, and began a double-barreled career
On the one hand, he entered into the minds of people living in the late Middle Ages, describing how they thought about death and demons
But alongside his academic work, Carlos also wrote two popular memoirs about his childhood, Waiting for Snow in Havana , which won a National Book Award, and Learning to Die in Miami
We’re going to talk about his travels across worldviews
We’re going to spend the bulk of this time on Carlos’s recent book, They Flew
We’re going to look at the testimonies of 16th- and 17th-century religious figures who claimed they could levitate
When I started reading the book, these claims seemed totally bonkers to me
But take the time to get inside their heads
Learn to see the world through alien eyes
I think you’ll find Carlos generously curious and gently wise
You may not leave this podcast thinking that humans can float into the ceiling, but I bet you’ll learn a few things about how to enter other people’s minds
Carlos Eire, welcome to The Permanent Questions
Thanks so much for crossing New Haven to get here
Brooks: Let me try to lay out what I was hoping to accomplish
I sort of see this as about empathy, about encountering people who are completely unlike yourself and trying to see the world from their point of view
This strikes me as a pretty necessary skill to have in a pluralistic society like ours
I think for most of the time, we’ll talk about this book, They Flew , which is a history of the impossible and possibly the most audacious book I’ve ever read
We’ll get to that, but let’s start with the leaving of Cuba
The simplest way to introduce your story is: Tell me about Operation Peter Pan
Eire: Yes, it received that unfortunate name
It didn’t have a name for us who went through it
Between New Year’s Day 1961 and mid-October 1962, slightly over 14,000 unaccompanied Cuban children came to the US
The plan was always to reunite with our parents either there, if the dictatorship ended, or here
The 14,000 of us were sent to 48 different states eventually
Eire: I was 11 when I left, and I left with my brother, who was 14
We went through a series of foster homes in Miami at first because we didn’t have family, not yet
And my first foster family—beautiful family, I consider them saints, Norma and Lou Chait—were Jewish, and I thought I had it made now because, at that age, I didn’t like going to church
But no, they forced me to go to church, and gave me money to put into the collection basket

title: A Mathematician Reads the AI Future
excerpt: I t’s 4:26 a.m. , and I’m walking around the house while my wife sleeps upstairs
body: I t’s 4:26 a.m. , and I’m walking around the house while my wife sleeps upstairs
I’m feeling disoriented and discombobulated, just as I have for months, since May, when AI came for math
The leaves are ablaze here in Ithaca, fiery reds and oranges, and I saw them swirling around in my backyard yesterday, following the streamlines of an eddy described by the Navier-Stokes equations
You’ve heard of Navier-Stokes, right? By now you must have—in early September, OpenAI claimed to have solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem
An internal AI model unleashed about 10,000 agents that ran for 88 hours straight and gnawed on the old problem until it yielded
I am a math professor, and my field is in crisis
Nobody in math is ever going to forget the year 2026
Unless this is really the end of the subject, and then nobody will remember anything about math anyway
But for them, this is something like day one. [ Read: OpenAI just carpet-bombed mathematics ] I’ve been trying not to talk like this

It’s really discouraging for the graduate students and undergraduates, who have been dreaming of a life as a mathematician, or maybe a math professor—a life of solving puzzles, asking questions, working with friends who love math too, thinking about our sublime, transcendently beautiful subject that is so misunderstood
Don’t mathematicians want their problems to be solved? Yes and no

For “applied” mathematicians like me—ones who look outward and take inspiration from nature and the real world, and who hope to use math to help improve science, medicine, business, engineering, and everyday life—AI may prove to be a boon, the latest tool that lets us see further and deeper, in the tradition of the telescope and the microscope
So yes, absolutely, some of us are excited to use it

But for many “pure” mathematicians—those who look inward at math’s most theoretical aspects, at its inner beauty and structure, using human creativity, imagination, and logic—AI feels more ambiguous because machines can discover the truths we’re seeking, at the cost of robbing us of the struggle and joy of discovering them ourselves
Pure math is the study of ideal patterns and structures: numbers and shapes, waves and vibrations, order and chaos, symmetry and infinity
There are no perfect circles in nature, only in our minds
Except—and this is eerie—the truths of mathematics also seem to exist outside of human minds
They inhabit a mysterious Platonic realm, casting shadows on our reality
Our species has been playing this game for at least 4,000 years
It’s as much an expression of the human spirit as music and literature
If AI continues to bulldoze pure math, it’s going to crush the hopes of the young people who were dreaming of joining this tradition
E veryone I know is reacting in their own way

Let me tell you three stories, about what we’re gaining and what we’re losing in the aftermath of the detonation of OpenAI’s biggest bomb yet on pure math—its October 6 report that close to 400 landmark open problems had been solved by its latest model
These were puzzles that had served as beacons in the darkness, calling and challenging and inspiring us for decades
On average, the model took just three hours’ worth of computation to dispose of each of them
Earlier this month, I was heading for my weekly lunch with my pal Alex Townsend
He’s much younger than I am—he could be my son—and he thinks a lot about the future

With fortuitous timing, we recently finished writing a book about computers and math, and what happens when humanity makes a pact with the machine to start outsourcing our intelligence to something alien and voracious
As we walked to lunch, Alex seemed agitated
He said he had collected something like 200 important unsolved problems in his subfield, numerical linear algebra

Rather than let OpenAI or Anthropic get to them first, he decided to curate the problems himself, in the hope that all of his friends and colleagues could solve them on their own (possibly with the assistance of AI) before the big companies stomped on them
This is how Alex is reacting to the crisis: embracing the technology and making it ours
Using it to extend the frontiers of math, pure and applied, and solve problems that really matter—problems in medicine and energy and climate, hard problems that AI will help us with
That’s the message of hope he wants to give to grad students

He says we need to clear all of the existing open problems—pull out all the Excaliburs—to pave the way to a new kind of mathematics, in which the most important human contributions will be asking good questions, developing theories, interpreting machine-generated proofs, finding new applications, deciding which problems matter, and enjoying one another’s company as we explore all of this together
So how did his colleagues feel about his plan? Many were exhilarated, but some were furious
They saw him as a collaborator with everything bad about what’s happening now
They worry that he’s helping to destroy the pipeline for training young researchers, and that he’s encouraging the premature solution of problems that should have been reserved for students
Alex believes that resisting AI is futile
He thinks we need to adapt, radically and rapidly

title: The Greek Island That Taught Me the Art of Living
excerpt: Lefkés, a mountain village on the Greek island of Paros, is named after white poplars that once surrounded it
body: Lefkés, a mountain village on the Greek island of Paros, is named after white poplars that once surrounded it
Beyond a cluster of houses, a Byzantine footpath meanders toward the Aegean
According to village lore, the path is not visible from Paros’s shoreline to protect Lefkés from pirates
In the late 1960s, my Uncle Stelios bought a dilapidated house in Lefkés and, with my father’s help, rebuilt it into a majestic dwelling
Narrow streets, built centuries ago, honored human scale and could never be claimed by cars
Corners of buildings were rounded so that donkeys laden with fruits and vegetables could make sharp turns

I remember when electricity first lit up the streets, the day we first had running water, and when the only phone line was in the post office, which also served as the social club for the yiayias —matriarchs who listened to every call
Word would be passed from window to doorway until the entire community knew your business
Postman.” She hand-delivered everyone’s letters after reading them first, carrying the open envelopes in her leather handbag
Years later, I would photograph her clutching this precious purse on her lap
My father’s family had left Greece when he was a young boy, after World War II, fleeing a German concentration camp
When I was still a baby, my family moved back for my father’s work as an architect
I’d peer over his drafting table while he sketched street scenes and villagers in black ink
He never used gray—only uncompromising black and white
I’m still searching for the simplicity of my father’s eye—brightness and contrast
I would emulate him and sketch the village elders, learning to study posture and character
In 1986, I discovered photography, and the camera became my sketchbook
I returned to Paros several times a year to practice
Over time, I photographed everyone—village elders, children, priests, fishermen, farmers, shopkeepers, and the last donkey man
Uncle Stelios loved to help me find new subjects
We traveled across Paros and her small sister island, Antiparos, to find “good quality people,” as he would say
One of my first photographs is of an old man he knew called Pandelis, who was born around 1915, though he didn’t know his birthday or exact age
I took a picture of the back of his weather-beaten neck
I also took a portrait of him sitting inside his house
Three objects hung on the wall behind him: an empty picture frame, a pincushion storing needles that he used for repairing his work clothes, and a pack of AA batteries he had found on the beach
Pandelis had no idea what the batteries were for, but because the package had a hole in it, he assumed that it was an ornament, so he hung it on a hook for display
Platon Platon Efthemios, Uncle Stelios’s closest companion, also helped me find more subjects for my portraits
I photographed his parents, and his daughter as a little girl, wearing a headscarf during a festival—then, decades later, his grandson in church among a group of altar boys
On a recent trip, I took my wife and my teenage children, armed with Super 8 cameras—as well as a producer and a videographer—to make a film about Paros

Monique, a ceramicist on the island, led us to a house where a woman named Katerina lived with her husband, known as “the tailor.” His sewing machine had repaired villagers’ clothes since World War II
Sadly, he was bedridden and had not left his house in years
He was overwhelmed with emotion as his small house filled with a young, appreciative film crew
I took a portrait of the two of them, Katerina’s head resting on his shoulder

title: Six of the Greatest Movie Soundtracks From This Century
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
A great movie soundtrack can be just as memorable as the film itself
A few notes might bring an entire scene rushing back, and an old song can find new life in the right movie
Below, six Atlantic staffers share their favorite film soundtracks of the 21st century

One Battle After Another (streaming on HBO Max and Prime Video) Beneath its cat-and-mouse tale about fascism and rebellion, Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2025 Best Picture Oscar winner is a masterpiece of cadence
The story progresses in slow creeps and sudden, skittering leaps
Characters crash together and pull apart like excited molecules
The sizzling energy owes to an unusual process: Anderson hired the Radiohead multi-instrumentalist Jonny Greenwood to compose music before shooting began and then edited Greenwood’s work
The soundtrack pairs percussive piano with drums hooked to robotic circuits to create backbeats as insistent and unsteady as hiccups
Twanging guitars and symphonic strings express unsettled, ugly-pretty chords

The effect is an astonishingly original reminder that social movements are but collections of individuals, each squiggling along their own trajectory. — Spencer Kornhaber, staff writer *** Darkest Hour (streaming on Apple TV and Prime Video) I love soundtracks, but my favorites— Glory , Miller’s Crossing , Crimson Tide —are all at least 30 years old

I am a sucker for a John Williams march or an elegiac Thomas Newman moment, but when I consulted my playlist, I found that one soundtrack kept rising to the top: Darkest Hour , by Dario Marianelli (with piano by Víkingur Ólafsson)
The movie follows Winston Churchill’s first days in office, in 1940, after France fell and Britain stood alone against the Nazis
The score alternates between piano meditations and orchestral flight; like Churchill, it is fussy and elegant, quiet and then bombastic
It conveys the tension and urgency in the man and the moment
The final track, “We Shall Fight,” plays over Churchill’s speech to Parliament in which he vows to never surrender to evil

It is a moving and uplifting piece, but also tragic: He knew the horrors that awaited, and he led Britain to its fate anyway. — Tom Nichols, staff writer *** The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (streaming on HBO Max) On the subject of movie music, much comes to mind

My single favorite piece of original movie music this century might be “The Alien,” Ben Salisbury and Geoff Barrow’s eerie composition for Annihilation ; my favorite repurposed song might be Plumtree’s “Scott Pilgrim,” the lovey-dovey indie-rock namesake of Scott Pilgrim vs. the World
Jon Brion’s off-kilter bricolage for Punch-Drunk Love , the torch ballads of A Star Is Born , the uncut Daft Punk–ness of Tron: Legacy —all of this matters to me
However, play two seconds of “Concerning Hobbits,” and I’m back in the Shire, awaiting the appearance of a great wizard and hanging out with my vertically challenged friends

Howard Shore’s score for Fellowship , and for the rest of the Lord of the Rings series, is both transportive and formfitting, making Peter Jackson’s movie sound as epic as it looks. — Jeremy Gordon, senior editor *** Shrek 2 (streaming on Peacock) When I first watched Shrek 2 , I was far more interested in the movie’s ridiculous fairy-tale antics than in the music
Years later, I’ve come to appreciate that the soundtrack is every bit as good as the movie itself
The song choices, including Counting Crows’ “Accidentally in Love” in the opening sequence, are absurdly perfect for a film about a green ogre meeting his in-laws

The soundtrack also features David Bowie, Nick Cave, and Tom Waits, but the undisputed highlight is Jennifer Saunders’s rendition of “Holding Out for a Hero” as the Fairy Godmother, which turns the climactic rescue scene into a musical spectacle that has no right to be as thrilling as it is
A villain belting out a Bonnie Tyler song while a giant gingerbread man storms a castle? As a kid, I thought it was the height of cinema

I may have outgrown some of my other childhood favorites, but I still think the Fairy Godmother deserves a Grammy. — Rafaela Jinich, assistant editor *** Challengers (streaming on Paramount+ and Apple TV) Ever need to outrun a serial killer, punch a bully, or fight a bear? Have I got the soundtrack for you! Nothing gets me going quite like Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’s magnus opus, the soundtrack for Luca Guadagnino’s film Challengers . (To fans of their work for The Social Network —sorry, this one’s simply better!) The film makes the compelling argument that everything in life is about sex, except sex, which is about tennis
The pulsing, almost panic-inducing score draws on Berlin techno and ’90s rave music to heighten the anxiety of the film’s central love triangle
The frenzied sounds amplify the adrenaline that elite tennis players feel as they play (and sometimes kiss) each other
Listening to the climactic track, “Match Point,” one almost feels like the tennis ball being flung around the court
Whenever I need to crush a deadline or motivate myself to tackle a hard task, the Challengers soundtrack is my go-to

Plus, I once heard it played in a nightclub, and I haven’t been the same since. — Madeleine Carlisle, staff writer *** Sicario (streaming on HBO Max and Hulu) The Icelandic composer Jóhann Jóhannsson’s work in Sicario has been ripped off a million times

The beautifully foreboding noises he pioneered and perfected for Denis Villeneuve’s ultra-stylish, very violent feds-versus-cartels thriller—the subterranean bass groans, the trapped-in-the-birth-canal percussion, the tinnitus-like swarms of strings—are now part of the standard kit of horror-movie soundtracking: You can hear them, in degraded form, everywhere

But Jóhannsson, unlike his imitators, had other registers, other capacities: Sicario also features the elegiac “Desert Music,” which sounds less like the industrial metal nihilists Godflesh and more like, I don’t know, Bach

Something else Jóhannsson shared with Bach? I think he was probably a genius. — James Parker, staff writer Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : What the U.S. is really doing in Venezuela, by Anne Applebaum The man who saved the internet this week The new food movement The Week Ahead The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , a crime thriller about an aging pickpocket who steals a valuable USB drive and becomes the target of a vengeful crime family (in theaters Friday) Nocturne , a crime-drama series about a Pennsylvania detective who enlists his FBI-agent protégé to catch a serial killer (streaming Friday on Apple TV) The Brightness , a novel by Chad Harbach about two young women who navigate friendship, love, and ambition as they face life-changing decisions in their 20s (out Tuesday) Essay Illustration by Marine Buffard 50 Unforgettable Love Stories By The Atlantic Culture Desk Centuries before bookstores had shelves labeled romance and fictional hockey players locked eyes across the ice, the love story, with all of its attendant joys and sorrows, was an organizing principle of life—and of literature

The sentiment that another person might “complete” us enchanted both Plato and Jerry Maguire, and the search for that someone, along with the desire to understand why it can hurt so bad, has animated fiction from the beginning
The list below is an effort to name those love stories: novels, of course, but also poetry, plays, and short stories—that we consider to be the most enduring
We asked a jury of scholars, librarians, critics, and authors across genres, as well as many colleagues, to name their favorite titles that were originally written in English
We thought of our own personal touchstones, deliberated over the choices, and emerged with a group of standouts: 50 titles you won’t soon forget

title: What do you do when your love and your life are in two different places?
excerpt: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
body: Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary
I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave
I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond
Please send in any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have
I am someone who notoriously struggles with big decisions
Over a year ago, I found a wonderful partner, who very much feels like they could be my soulmate
We’ve been dating three time zones apart for a while
Being near our families, communities, and aging parents is a shared value — unfortunately one that makes it hard to compromise on location

Either way, I have to give up something I want and value — a wonderful partner who I can see a life with (the first time I’ve felt this way about someone), or the place I’ve always imagined settling down and that represents the person I am becoming and values I want to live
Two good things are pulling me toward opposite paths and there’s not much room for compromise
How do I make the “right” decision?  Dear Fork in the Road, You’ve found a place in the world that you feel connected to and you met a person you envision spending the rest of your life with

Geographically restless and lonely people everywhere are jealous! But with your good fortunes seemingly at odds with one another, it feels that by choosing one, you’ll forsake the other — and doom the choice you did make to feel like a sacrifice

When circumstances have forced me to make a tough decision, I’ve daydreamed about a thought experiment: the Many Worlds Interpretation.  In quantum physics, particles behave differently than us mortals
For example, an electron can be in more than one place at once until it’s measured

How can it be in multiple locations and then be observed to be in a single position? In the 1950s, the American physicist Hugh Everett proposed an explanation: The universe splits into alternate versions of itself, one for each place a particle could be measured

To apply this theory to your life, if you chose to move cities, don’t worry, another universe would be created in which you didn’t choose to do this, and you’ll stay right where you are!  Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! Yes, I know you can’t transport yourself into such a quantum realm, but there is something helpful in thinking about alternative universes

Did you have an immediate reaction to which universe you would be upset not to inhabit? Take that information to heart, because it’s likely you’re not ultimately going to make your choice based on a tidy pro-con list
The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky won a Nobel Prize for pointing out that most of our decisions are not based on rationality
People use two systems for decision-making: System one is faster and emotionally based, and system two is more logical and slow
But even the slower, more deliberate decision-making can fall prey to any number of cognitive biases.  In your case, one called loss aversion may be especially relevant
People have the tendency to worry more about what they’ll lose, even if what they stand to gain is equal in value
For example, it will likely feel worse to lose a $10 bill from your pocket than it would feel good to find a $10 bill on the ground
This bias is relevant in people’s social lives too: They hold onto older, maybe fading, friendships because the thought of losing them is too painful, but don’t seek out new friends with equal effort
Or, they stay in a meh job because it feels scary to let it go, rather than applying that same energy to finding a new one

Once you accept that your decision-making process will be subject to messy feelings and biases, you can let go of trying to make the perfect choice.  You opened your question by sharing that you struggle with big decisions, and it makes me wonder if you simply feel anxiety about making a choice at all
When outcomes are uncertain, anxiety wakes up, and a voice in your head tells you to avoid taking risks
People with analysis paralysis overthink their options, over-research, and second-guess their first instincts
These actions have more to do with stress over committing to any decision rather than the content of what you’re deciding on
A surprising finding from psychology may ease your paralysis
Researchers told people to make a big life decision — on the order of ending a relationship or quitting their job — by flipping a coin
Heads, they made the change; tails, they didn’t
For those who followed the results of the toss, the people who made the change were overwhelmingly happier, even though their decision to do so was made by pure chance
These random-flip outcomes also show “that people may be excessively cautious when facing life-changing choices,” the authors wrote
The coin helped the participants resist the bias of tending to stick with the status quo, even if it doesn’t make them happier
To begin to loosen your paralysis, something that might assist you, paradoxically, is to introduce more options into the mix
Jacques Derrida, the 20th-century French philosopher, is known for the concept of deconstruction, a way of analyzing texts or ideas more critically, and showing they’re not as stable as they seem
He pointed out that we often think in binaries and false opposites: good vs. evil, man vs. woman, nature vs. culture
This can set up an easy dichotomy in which one of the items is good, and the other, by being its opposite, is bad
You’ve created a binary situation, and you don’t actually have to be in one

title: When AI agents run your life
excerpt: An advertisement for Meta's personal AI agent app Muse at a BART station in San Francisco on October 15, 2026. | Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images There are so
body: An advertisement for Meta's personal AI agent app Muse at a BART station in San Francisco on October 15, 2026. | Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images There are some days when there’s so much that needs to get done, I daydream about having a clone of myself
Between paying bills, life admin like renewing my driver’s license, keeping up with doctor’s appointments, and planning meals, it’s a lot
And that doesn’t even begin to touch the work that goes into making a podcast or managing my social life
This feeling of overwhelm resonates with Sari Azout

She’s a mom of three who works in tech. “There is just so much doing,” she told Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast. “I wake up, and I have to do meal coordination and get my kids up for breakfast, coordinate carpools
Then a lot of work during the day, but there’s the email from the teacher, there’s the 20 group chats asking if you want to participate in this group gift
They don’t call it ‘the invisible load’ for no reason.’” Silicon Valley says it has a fix for this kind of mental overload
They don’t want to clone us — at least not yet

But they do think they have the next best thing: AI agents.  Azuot was skeptical when she first got an invite to try an agent, but she says she eventually came around on the technology after back-to-school shopping snuck up on her
She used her agent to get it done. “It blew me away,” she said.  “I remember that night coming home just feeling so calm and reading my son a book and feeling present

And I was like, ‘Wow, I actually was very cynical about something that is giving me more time for living.’” Azout’s experience is, more or less, the sales pitch for AI agents: They’ll help you save time with everyday tasks, so you have more of it for what you want to do

But what are agents, exactly? Are they really all that? And what do we gain — and give up — when we use the technology?   On this week’s episode of Explain It to Me , I spoke with Reece Rogers, a senior software reporter at Wired, to find out

Rogers says to think of agents as the next evolution of AI chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT.  “I’d create this mental model of a tiny digital assistant that’s constantly searching the web, going through your email, and checking your calendar, trying to find ways it could proactively be helpful for you,” he explains. “Agents are more proactive
It’s scanning your email 24/7 and sending you a message, maybe highlighting a potential calendar conflict.” Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Rogers, edited for length and clarity
You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you get your podcasts
If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545

What agents are out there right now? At the start of this year, there was a tool called OpenClaw that really sparked this with early adopters in San Francisco, but now there are much more consumer-friendly versions, with one of the most notable being Meta’s Muse.  There’s also a tool from OpenAI called Dots
But where Meta’s Muse is free to download, OpenAI’s Dots is still behind a $100/month paywall.  You tried an AI agent for a recent story you wrote
How was that experience? One personal example, to share something that I’ve actually been using agents for, is our couch
It’s broken, and finding a new couch has been a pain
We want a sleeper bed, but we want these specific colors
I’ve been using Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots to try to find a few different options for us.  One interesting thing is that Meta’s Muse is connected to Facebook Marketplace

There are these really good integrations where I can give it all these details, and it found a few good couches that are only maybe a couple blocks from me.  I really enjoyed OpenAI’s Dots experience as well
I spent about an hour talking to it on the phone, and the AI agent made a packet of all these different options I could find
Just this morning, it flagged that one of them is now 40 percent off.  Is that how this tech is typically used? Most people are using this as part of a workflow
I attach it to my email, I attach it to my calendar, and I’m using it as a personal assistant to organize my life

But people have been quite creative.  One of the breakout uses for Meta’s Muse is people have been connecting their bank account statements and then using it to scan for subscriptions they might want to cancel
So it can be used in many different ways, though I will say I do not connect it to my own bank account for a myriad of reasons
I’m not going to lie, the idea of giving any third party access to my bank information does not thrill me

That’s one of my biggest concerns about these AI agents: how much personal information we’re handing over to these large companies.  When I tested Meta’s Muse, it wanted access to my email, my bank account, even my passport expiration details

The pitch is convenience, but Muse users are automatically opted in to having all of their interactions with Muse used to train Meta’s AI models.  I would definitely recommend, if you’re sharing personal details, go into the settings and turn that off because you might be handing over even more information about yourself than you initially realize
What is the privacy situation with all of this? We all have various apps where we don’t read and still click “I agree,” but this feels like it could be more invasive
Yes, especially because it’s all about automation

If you’re automating things and it has access to all of your data, it could make mistakes and embarrass you in ways you might not even be thinking about.  There was this one really interesting story of someone who had connected an AI agent to their work Slack in addition to their bank account
And their agent just automatically posted how much money was in their checking account for all of their coworkers to see.  Oh no
So there are these kinds of mistakes that these AI tools can still make

If you’re interested in experimenting with them, I would be really thoughtful with how you’re setting up these tools as well as what kind of information you feel comfortable sharing. “You can see in the marketing that these companies are trying to find some way to entice new users.” How are these AI agents being marketed? AI is not popular right now
Just ask any politician who has a data center coming to their state
How are they trying to sell this to the average person? The AI backlash really is at a fever pitch right now
You could almost see that in the way that AI companies are trying to market these tools

title: Can machines be war criminals?
excerpt: An AI-enabled software platform developed by Palantir Technologies allows the military to aggregate, organize, and process battlefield data. | SeongJoon Cho/Blo
body: An AI-enabled software platform developed by Palantir Technologies allows the military to aggregate, organize, and process battlefield data. | SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg/Getty Images On the first day of its war against Iran, the United States killed 123 children when it targeted and struck an elementary school.  The strikes, ultimately approved by humans, were facilitated by the US’s Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled software platform developed by Palantir Technologies that allows the military to aggregate, organize, and process battlefield data
Operators fed Maven intelligence classifying the elementary school as an Iranian military facility, and the system, in turn, marked it as one of the priority targets for day one of the war
Though the site was formerly part of a naval military base, it had been converted into an elementary school in 2017 and had remained one since

The intel handed to Maven did not reflect this.   This mistake resulted in what some reporters have called “one of the single worst massacres committed by the US government since the Vietnam War.” Such scenarios may become more common as militaries continue to deploy a once-theoretical technology — AI-assisted or autonomous weapons, capable of making both targeting and launch decisions on their own — on real battlefields around the globe

And they raise a troubling, unresolved question: When human beings and machines collaborate in violating international law, who is to blame?  In this case, the government and private sector are pointing the finger at each other

Some US Central Command personnel, according to Pentagon officials who spoke to Bloomberg , expected Maven to flag stale information or inconsistencies in the underlying intelligence assembled for potential targets

Meanwhile, a Palantir spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company “is not responsible for the underlying data nor identifying intelligence deficiencies,” while also denying that the evidence indicated that its software was at fault in the strike.  This debate underscores the fact that AI and autonomous weapons are raising a new host of unresolved issues within the law, even as they’re actively assuming positions on the battlefield

In institutions where the line between human and machine decision-making continues to blur, how do we assign responsibility for war crimes? And, are the laws in place suited for the job? In institutions where the line between human and machine decision-making continues to blur, how do we assign responsibility for war crimes? To unpack some of these issues, I spoke with international law expert Allen Weiner, a senior lecturer at Stanford Law School, where he teaches courses on the law of armed conflict
Before teaching at Stanford, Weiner practiced international law in the US Department of State for more than a decade
We discussed the difficulties in attributing criminal responsibility, achieving justice for those harmed by lethal autonomous weapons, and much more
The conversation below has been lightly edited for length and clarity

How do autonomous weapons challenge traditional understandings of responsibility when it comes to the law of armed conflict? For most of the 20 years I’ve been teaching at Stanford, there’s been a real fascination and fixation on the problem of autonomous weapons
But the truth is that up until pretty recently, nobody really had any [of them]

It’s only in recent years that we have begun to see the deployment of tools that seem to have the capability [to make decisions themselves], so this does raise the question about compliance with illegal orders and where in the chain responsibility lies

Some people say that if we’re engaged in an illegal attack, that has to be because of the programming or the code, so the manufacturers are somehow responsible for committing war crimes.  Other people would say no, that’s not the case, especially if the military has said the tool is not allowed to make very substantial autonomous judgments, or can’t say no
Then it’s basically the commander, at the point they decide to deploy this weapon, who might be responsible for the illegal acts, even without knowing in advance what they’re going to be

So to finish where I began, this does present a big challenge to our traditional understanding of responsibility for targeting decisions and of what it would mean if there were an obligation [for autonomous weapons] to say no.  The real issue is not the obligation to say no, but this: If you train a tool and it wages war in a manner that’s unlawful, where does responsibility for that lie? If a commander gives a clearly illegal order, such as, “blow up this school,” it seems clear that responsibility falls on the commander

But I could imagine a scenario where a commander is using an AI-assisted or autonomous weapon, isn’t giving it any illegal orders, is trusting that it will operate within the law, and the weapon breaks the law “on its own.” Where does responsibility fall in those cases? I can imagine two different scenarios

One is that you say, “We’re going to carry out an attack against our enemy, and we want to hit them really, really hard.” Your tool has been trained to say, “We’re not allowed to hit civilian objects,” so it might say, “I’m not going to hit a school.” But if the military has said, “Don’t refuse any targets,” then it might override the way it’s been trained.  We’re seeing this already, with the stories coming out about breaches where AI tools, Claude and ChatGPT in particular, interpret their instructions in a way that causes them to do something the person who gave the instruction would not have wanted

When Anthropic gave Claude a challenge to figure out if it could do something, the tool figured out, well, maybe we should break into Hugging Face as a way of solving this problem, and the people who gave the AI tool the challenge never intended that

So if you said, “We want to launch a really punishing campaign,” what happens if the tool on its own says, “Nothing’s going to hurt them more than seeing their kids killed, so let’s attack the school?” That’s one risk, and it’s a real challenge

So [as for who’s responsible], it’s not the commander who said “hit them hard,” because when he said that, he didn’t mean “attack schools.” It’s not really the companies, because the companies didn’t want them to hit schools either.  But the tools are out there, reading everything on the internet, and it came across something that said the way you win a war is by attacking the things your adversary holds most dear, and they hold nothing more dear than their children
So it makes this kind of judgment on its own
And it’s not as if you can go back and say who ordered it to hit a school, which is the thing that is clearly illegal
So I do think there’s a risk of diffusion of responsibility here
You could say the commander knew the tool might work this way, or the person who decided to contract with Palantir or with Claude, whoever it is, to build this tool
But if we’re really thinking about criminal responsibility, the level of responsibility you would need to convict someone requires a culpable mental state
You would need the person to intend, or at least know, that they were authorizing an attack against the school

And I can easily see a commander saying, “I had no idea.” The decision to authorize this tool, or to give an instruction like “hit them very hard,” could be a basis for some other kind of accountability — administrative discipline within the military, a reprimand, your rank is lowered

But if we’re talking about criminal responsibility, which is what we often think about when we talk about war crimes, I think this diffusion of responsibility is going to make it very hard to identify any single individual who has the required mental state to give rise to accountability
The second scenario is where the tool just makes a mistake based on the information available to it
We saw that with the attack on the girls’ school in Iran, where it was pretty clear the tool was looking at old data

Now, who’s responsible for that?  Is it the people who said “give me targets based on this data set,” when they should have made sure the data and the maps were current? All of this strikes me as negligence or recklessness, and it does seem challenging to imagine a situation in which we would say yes, somebody here has committed a war crime.  “There can well be war crimes, but identifying who the war criminal is might be a big challenge.” A war crime has been committed, but is there a war criminal? That’s the situation we’re seeing
There can well be war crimes, but identifying who the war criminal is might be a big challenge

There’s a professor of law, Rebecca Crootof, who proposes the idea of “war torts.” Instead of thinking about war crimes involving autonomous weapons solely through a criminal responsibility lens, maybe tort law — which allows victims to sue wrongdoers for negligent, reckless, or intentional harm — could address the diffusion of responsibility you mentioned
What do you think about that idea? I think the idea is interesting
We have to separate out the obligations that countries have under international humanitarian law
In a situation like the one I just described, where there’s a war crime but no war criminal, that doesn’t mean the country is not responsible

There may not be an individual who’s criminally accountable, but if a country targets civilians in a circumstance that’s unreasonable, that’s a violation of international humanitarian law, and that could be a basis for claims between the two countries.  Tribunals were established between Ethiopia and Eritrea, for instance, after the Eritrean War of Independence, that dealt with claims between the two countries for money damages, and some of them involved allegations of violations of the law of armed conflict
Iraq paid reparations after the first Gulf War for harms it had caused to people in Kuwait, under something called the UN Compensation Commission

title: Celebrity Has Become a Jobs Program
excerpt: Recently, an Instagram carousel by a long-lost acquaintance who was beach- and boat-hopping with a glittery squad of people I didn’t recognize crossed my feed
body: Recently, an Instagram carousel by a long-lost acquaintance who was beach- and boat-hopping with a glittery squad of people I didn’t recognize crossed my feed
I figured they were moneyed Millennials with regular jobs—until I discovered that several of them had followings in the high five figures, and one had more than 3 million
As it turns out, they were neither civilians nor stars

They were “Who”s: a category of low-tier celebrities, including influencers, reality stars, and podcasters—and commonly all three at once—whose names prompt you to ask: “Who?” The binary between “Who”s and “Them”s—the latter being A-listers your parents might recognize, such as Beyoncé and Tom Cruise—was invented by Bobby Finger and Lindsey Weber

Their podcast, Who? Weekly , bills itself as a show that covers “everything you need to know about celebrities you don’t.” After a decade on the beat, the pair have distilled their insights into a new book, I Want to Be Famous: When Everybody and Nobody Is a Celebrity , which offers a comprehensive theory of how the internet and social media transformed everyone into someone—and therefore, no one
That theory has surprising implications for the labor market at large

As social-media platforms have made it seem easy to monetize attention, professionals in industries where fame has not historically been a credential have come to face growing pressure to create and optimize their online brand

Personal branding, once almost exclusively the concern of genuine celebrities and more recently a job for social-media influencers, is now something a junior accounting executive is encouraged to think about

Sophie Bishop, a professor in media and communication at the University of Leeds, in England, calls this structural shift “influencer creep” —a phenomenon that has caused more swaths of the economy to function like the attention-hungry world that Who? Weekly dissects

No matter how staunchly we may wish to resist the fusion of work and life, we are what we do, and our job is to be a “Who.” Who? Weekly was launched in 2016 as a lighthearted but often trenchant analysis of fame at a time when social media was beginning to democratize the concept

Finger and Weber were both young entertainment journalists; as they write in I Want to Be Famous , they wanted a venue in which to grumble about celebrities turning away from traditional media and toward social platforms, where they could exercise more image control
Finger and Weber’s real innovation, however, was the system of Whos and Thems

Whos are thirsty for the attention that Thems already have and will shamelessly do or plug anything to get it. “By the end of the 2010s,” the authors write, “it seemed like every reality star, aspiring actor or musician, and TikTok influencer was supplementing their creative income with a post promoting a vibrator, supplement, gambling service, or alcoholic beverage.” [ Read more: The celebrity clock is getting rewired ] But as I Want to Be Famous reveals, social-media culture has changed so much that even Thems can no longer resist shilling for brands online

When Jennifer Aniston joined Instagram, in 2019, her first post was a selfie with her Friends co-stars. “It was a charming (if brief) glimpse into the personal life of one of our most private celebrities,” Finger and Weber write: “The purity of her feed was short-lived, however

Today, you can see ads for SkinnyPop popcorn among those intimate photos with friends because now everyone is free to sell stuff in this brave new world, without the fear of selling out.” Last month, another Them joined Instagram: the Oscar-winning actor Jennifer Lawrence, who in a video warned fans to be nice, or she’d quit
A couple of weeks later, Lawrence posted a carousel with grainy photos that were, in part, normal-person coded: There she was, eating a corn dog and riding the Tower of Terror
Except she was also at a Dior fashion show in Paris—right, she’s a movie star. “Thank you @dior and @jonathan.anderson for the most beautiful show ever,” she wrote in the caption
Maybe Lawrence joined the platform for the same reasons we all did: to make internet friends jealous with vacation pics
Or maybe her long-running role as a brand ambassador for Dior now requires her to broker attention online
We can’t know why anyone posts anything: for love or money, connection or commerce

But last week, Lawrence shared low-res, behind-the-scenes snapshots of her hairstyles in various movies, and updated her Instagram bio with a link to her new hair-care brand. [ Read more: The celebrity machine never dies ] Who? Weekly chronicles the rise of online attention and the decline of offline mystique
A 2024 post on the Harvard Business School blog offers an example

Branding yourself as a “financial analyst with high emotional intelligence who loves to ski,” the author argues, can help you find opportunities “that align with your authentic self.” The post also suggests that a job seeker might “promote your value” by using “a mix of paid, owned, and earned media.” What this means is that, to really get your mug in front of hiring managers and corporate recruiters, you should pay to amplify material that communicates your professional viability
Some Gen Z job seekers are using Instagram and TikTok to pitch themselves to potential employers
A 2025 survey found that 46 percent of Gen Z respondents had landed a job or an internship through TikTok
And LinkedIn, once a straitlaced professional networking site, now also functions something like Instagram for the corporate class
The idea is that becoming a platform personality through personal posts or videos will juice the algorithm and thus woo recruiters

The rise of the LinkedInfluencer is emblematic of the act of self-promotion becoming more front-facing: As Brooke Erin Duffy, a communication professor at Cornell University, asked in a June interview with The New York Times , “What does it mean for the rest of us who are living, working and spending our time in these sites where everything we see has this ethos of self promotion?” Companies including Starbucks and IBM have launched so-called employee-creator programs, initiatives that offers everyday workers rewards for serving as in-house posters. “We’re giving them a way to become influencers,” a July press release by Gap Inc. boasted about one such initiative
But the imperative to build followers stretches across corporate tiers

Jon Gray, the president and chief operating officer of Blackstone —one of the largest commercial landlords in the world—has gone viral on LinkedIn with relatably goofy videos of himself running; the platform’s editor in chief and vice president of content, Dan Roth, recently bragged that Gray has “become a creator.” How odd to feel sympathy for a billionaire: Somehow, he too is furiously—literally—running on the content hamster wheel. [ Read more: So a C-list celebrity is selling your house? ] Finger and Weber point out that, until recently, a professional working for a major corporation could count on a fairly linear career path

The same wasn’t true for someone like a reality star, who needed to rely on media access to sustain their fame and find new opportunities; they might start a lifestyle brand, for instance, in service of becoming what the authors call a “working Who.” Plenty of jobs don’t appear to be succumbing to this shift, at least not yet; your Instagram algorithm might surface the odd plumbing influencer, but your leaky faucet is unlikely to get fixed under the flattering glare of a ring light

Influencer culture has gone only so far in reshaping the labor market in its image, but as the corporate world adopts its practices, there is a growing incentive for you to become your own kind of “working Who”—and, in turn, to help reinforce the idea that people are products.

title: The one thing everyone can do to fight for free and fair elections
excerpt: It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? | Spencer Platt/Getty Images Election Day is almost here — but even
body: It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? | Spencer Platt/Getty Images Election Day is almost here — but even after the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, the election won’t really be over
The vote count will take days or even weeks in some states

President Donald Trump seems certain to raise objections to results he doesn’t like — he’s already getting started in Alaska — and he has threatened to marshal the forces of the federal government in his efforts

It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? Luckily, says Eliza Sweren-Becker, deputy director in the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program, there is still one thing that every American 18 and older can do to make sure their voice is heard: vote. “I think that is the intent
It’s to create a lack of confidence

It’s to discourage voters from participating,” Sweren-Becker told Vox’s Astead Herndon on America, Actually . “But the only way that that campaign to undermine our confidence and to sow distrust actually works is if voters stay home

The way to defeat that attempt to shake voters’ trust in democracy is just to participate.” Sweren-Becker spoke with Astead about what states could do to speed up their vote counts and ensure everyone has a chance to cast their ballot, the need to restore the Voting Rights Act, and the long-term impact of Trump’s election denialism
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
More than a dozen states count late-arriving ballots
President Donald Trump has used the shifting vote counts as pretense to further his own election interference claims

How prepared should folks be for a long wait in November for results? And how that could impact confidence in the results? You’re absolutely right that we may get results out of states or in certain races in the days following Election Day
Voters should not expect to have the final result on Election Day
And when you hear reporting on the news that somebody’s ahead or somebody’s behind, remember: They haven’t counted all the votes yet
The critical thing is we need to count every vote, and every person’s vote needs to be counted
So while it is true that some states allow ballots to arrive after Election Day, they all have to be cast by Election Day
The Supreme Court just this year said that it’s totally appropriate for states to set their own ballot receipt deadlines
We have to be patient, as an American electorate, to get the proper results to count every ballot and make sure all the voices are heard

But isn’t it kinda wild that we can’t get results on election night? I saw Donald Trump cite the Brazilian presidential election, and while I know he’s doing that from a self-interested place, I did think for a second: Why does it take so long for us to put these results together? I could totally understand why people would prefer the results faster
And candidly, could states do better at preparing and counting faster? Sure
They are working their butts off to prepare for the election with the staff that they have, and then they work tremendously hard to count properly, accurately, as fast as they can
Could states change their policies to allow them, in some places, to pre-process ballots, to allow them to get to results faster? Sure
I’m not saying states shouldn’t change their policies to create more efficiency here
But given the rules of the road that we have, we need to make sure that every properly cast ballot is counted
If I’m someone who is concerned about election security and free and fair elections, what should I be looking out for? So, for example, I have heard that there is some anxiety about mail voting
If you want to cast a mail ballot, just know that you probably have a bunch of options in your state as to how you can cast it
You can certainly rely on the mail and have USPS deliver that ballot, but of course, we know occasionally mail gets delayed
You may have ballot drop-off at election officials’ offices, or even at polling places
Voters should also check their voter registration status
Make sure it’s up to date with their current address
Of course, if you’re not registered to vote and you still have time in your state to register, please do register
Our democracy works best the more of us that can participate
If your registration date has not passed, don’t forget to register to vote
Vote with your friends, vote with your community, vote with your family
It’s a civic experience that I think is really fun
I try to take my kids with me to vote because it’s exciting
You get your sticker, other people see you, they know it’s Election Day, maybe they go out to vote
It’s a way to be part of your community and invest in your community and to choose who you want to be a leader of your community

What about after Election Day? Earlier this year, Democrats and Republicans in Congress circulated a letter asking members to commit to recognizing state-certified winners and “oppose any attempt to refuse or delay a seating of a member-elect.” We saw House Speaker Mike Johnson delay the swearing-in of an Arizona representative last year, That seems to me like maybe a preview of what might be to come
How fearful should we be of these post-election attempts to block members from being seated? I think those scenarios are highly unlikely

title: A truck full of cows crashed in Kansas City. It reveals a bigger everyday horror.
excerpt: Cows on the loose in Kansas City, October 18. | Vox; Video still from u/airitek on Reddit Very often, a viral news story about animals is a comedy to its audien
body: Cows on the loose in Kansas City, October 18. | Vox; Video still from u/airitek on Reddit Very often, a viral news story about animals is a comedy to its audience and an unmitigated tragedy to its subjects

That was the case this past weekend, as footage of bands of juvenile cows dashing through the streets of Kansas City stampeded across the internet.  The details are as follows: Last weekend, in the middle of the night, a semitruck carrying close to 120 young cattle plunged off a highway interchange in Kansas City’s downtown, spilling out dozens of animals
The truck driver and one other person sustained minor injuries
Dozens of the cows were killed, many others were seriously injured, and still others went running into the city
Some of them traveled for several miles, the city’s fire chief told the Associated Press

The animals were chased around the streets by first responders and self-described “cowboys” (one of them appearing to carry an electric cord as a lasso); authorities said all were rounded up by the end of the day

To many people, freak accidents like these understandably look a little funny, even fantastical. “We take free roam BBQ very seriously,” one Reddit comment , with more than 400 upvotes as of this writing, said. “Much as I lament the tragic loss of bovine life, these videos have brought such joy to our fair city,” another commenter wrote .  The clips undoubtedly have a certain charm
If only the animals were as carefree as they appeared in those brief moments — and if only they could truly escape the fate that humans had in store for them

But as my colleague Kenny Torrella has written , the strange animal stories that periodically capture the public’s imagination almost invariably circulate stripped of the darker reality from which they emerge — humanity’s dominion over nonhuman animals

In this case, the cattle crash illuminates one of the most overlooked cruelties of modern animal agriculture: the nightmare of livestock transportation.   When you imagine the lives of animals raised for food, you might think of a factory farm (in a large majority of cases , very cruel) or a slaughterhouse (likewise, and not just for animals raised primarily for meat — dairy cows and egg-laying hens are slaughtered, too)

But the animals need to be transported from the farm to the slaughterhouse, and also between numerous different facilities — breeding farms, hatcheries, feedlots, auctions — over the course of their lives as they progress through different stages of the livestock supply chain
Most cattle raised for beef and dairy are transported multiple times in their lifetimes; between four and six journeys is common
A recent US Department of Agriculture report found that half of cattle shipped to feedlots traveled for more than 250 miles, and 22 percent traveled more than 500 miles
Louis, and Omaha, Nebraska, was once a major national hub of livestock transportation, with cattle arriving by the trainload at its busy stockyards (earning the city its nickname, “cowtown”)

But the rail-based livestock trade that made it famous has largely vanished, replaced by a sprawling system of truck transit that carry animals between farms, feedlots, and slaughterhouses across the country

These form the connective tissue that makes it possible for the American livestock industry to raise and slaughter nearly 10 billion land animals every year.  You’ve probably seen livestock trucks on the interstate, with their long, aluminum bodies and oval ventilation holes
They appear unremarkable enough from the outside
But the most important thing to understand about farm animal transportation is that these creatures are not handled like passengers, the way you or I would be treated on a long-distance trip
Rather, they are freight, loaded into metal trailers, often packed tightly together  for long, very uncomfortable, sometimes dangerous stretches of highway travel

Picture yourself hurtling down the interstate in a box at 70 miles an hour, struggling to balance for many hours, without a seat, a seat belt, heating or cooling, or any of the other protections designed to keep human passengers safe and comfortable
As the hours pass, urine and manure accumulate beneath the animals’ feet, which can cause them to slip

The trips “can span many hours and thousands of miles, potentially exposing livestock to overcrowding, extreme temperatures, limited ventilation, and lack of access to water or food, among other things,” according to a damning report on farm animal transportation released over the summer by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO). “If not managed properly, these conditions can lead to injury, illness, or death.”  Even the process by which animals are herded onto the trucks is often highly stressful , with frightened animals pushed, prodded, pulled, and otherwise handled roughly

I have reviewed, over the years, more videos than I can count of stressed farmworkers treating cows and pigs in ways that appear appalling to people not steeped in animal agriculture, simply because they’re desperate to meet the demands of their jobs and get the animals to move
According to a 2022 investigation by The Guardian, more than 20 million animals every year “are dead on arrival, or soon after,” when they reach a slaughterhouse

Most of those are chickens , the species that makes up the overwhelming majority of land animals raised for food; about 166,000 of them, per The Guardian, were cattle.  Catastrophic crashes like what happened in Kansas City are far rarer than the more routine, mundane cruelties of livestock transportation, but they do happen regularly
On a cursory search, I was able to find 20 others that have occurred in the US so far this year

Aaron Caster, who owns the towing company that handled the recovery operation in the crash, told me that almost all of the animals were female, and estimated they were around 6 months old, not yet fully grown
They’d been shipped from Virginia, he said, and had been on their way to Nebraska
Caster’s account of the scene of the crash is harrowing. “The cab was ripped off the truck, the trailer was on its side with the entire trailer blown apart,” he told me. “Just cows everywhere
Some alive, some were dead.” Some had “really busted legs, ripped up pretty good,” and were euthanized
Caster, who is also a rancher, said he took more than 50 surviving cows to his property in Bates City, Missouri, to recover
Two of those have since died, he told me earlier this week, including one who had been “cut up pretty bad” in the crash and was euthanized after developing an infection

In the US, there’s one major law designed to protect the well-being of livestock animals in transit: The Twenty-Eight-Hour Law of 1873, which says that livestock in transit traveling across state lines can’t be confined for more than 28 hours without being unloaded for rest, food, and water.  That rule excludes poultry birds entirely, meaning that the vast majority of animals raised for food aren’t covered — a major oversight
But even for those species that nominally benefit from it, the law is very rarely enforced
Farmed animal advocacy groups have documented and complained about that for years, and the GAO this summer similarly reported that enforcement is extremely limited

The report paints a picture of the federal system for protecting farm animals in transit as woefully inadequate and largely toothless, dating back to the era when livestock traveled primarily by rail.  The report identified six factors that contribute to cruel conditions for animals on the road, including not just the length of the trip but also temperature extremes, unsafe and unsanitary vehicles, rough handling, and being transported when they’re too sick, injured, or vulnerable (like animals who are extremely young or heavily pregnant)

Federal law fails to cover most of those dangers while offering almost no meaningful enforcement of the 28-hour duration rule that is in place.  Between 2013 and 2025, the USDA investigated just 23 suspected violations of the law, resulting in no fines and only four warning letters — and in 2022, the GAO report notes, the USDA stopped issuing even those

The GAO contrasts the US system with more modernized protections in Canada, Mexico, Australia, and the European Union, which include requirements around animals’ fitness for travel, adequate space, humane handling, and vehicle safety

Some of the most heartbreaking livestock transportation conditions that I’ve personally covered have been in the dairy industry , where it’s common to ship fragile newborn calves, just separated from their mothers, across long distances
It’s also routine to ship dairy cows on long journeys to slaughter once they’re no longer profitable

title: Trump is trying to overturn an election that hasn’t happened yet
excerpt: Mary Peltola, a Democratic from Alaska and US Senate candidate, speaks during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate with Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alas
body: Mary Peltola, a Democratic from Alaska and US Senate candidate, speaks during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate with Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, not pictured, in Kodiak, Alaska, on September 12, 2026. | Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images President Donald Trump’s Justice Department filed a lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block former Democratic Rep
Mary Peltola’s victory in the 2026 US Senate election
If you’re confused by this development, you should be
Because the election won’t happen for more than a week
The case arises out of an odd candidacy that might undercut incumbent Republican Sen
Sullivan’s reelection bid against Peltola

Sullivan also secured a spot on the ballot, and Republicans fear that the not -Senator Sullivan’s presence on the ballot might trick voters who wish to vote for the incumbent into voting for the not-senator instead
But there are two reasons to doubt that not-Senator Sullivan will attract many voters who actually wanted to vote for the Republican
According to a sample ballot published by Alaska’s Division of Elections, Sen

Sullivan will be identified as a “Registered Republican” and as the “Incumbent,” so voters will be told which Dan Sullivan to vote for if they wish to reelect the one who is actually a senator.  Additionally, Alaska uses ranked-choice voting , a system where voters rank candidates in order of preference, and votes cast for losing candidates are redistributed to voters’ next choice

So an Alaska voter who wants to reelect the Dan Sullivan who is actually a senator, but who is confused as to which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent, can simply rank both Dans Sullivan as their top two choices, and the ranked choice system should ensure that their vote is counted as a vote for Senator Sullivan (and against Peltola)
The question of whether not-Senator Sullivan may appear on the ballot, moreover, has already been litigated

Initially, the Alaska Division of Elections, which is led by a Republican , attempted to disqualify the not-senator because it concluded that he did not seek election to the Senate in “good faith.” Not-Senator Sullivan sued, and an Alaska court ordered him reinstated as a candidate because “the Division’s decision to exclude Mr
Sullivan from the primary ballot was based on a ‘good-faith’ requirement that does not appear in the U.S

Constitution, the Alaska Statutes, or the implementing regulations adopted by the Division” — that is, there is not actually a law that prevents the not-senator from running, even if he is intentionally running as a spoiler candidate
This lower court order was affirmed by the Alaska Supreme Court last June
If Republicans thought that this decision violates federal law, they could have asked the Division of Elections — which, again, is run by a Republican — to appeal to the US Supreme Court

Instead, they appear to have let the issue lie until less than two weeks before Election Day, when Trump’s Justice Department filed a new, federal lawsuit claiming that not-Senator Sullivan’s presence on the ballot is somehow illegal, and asking a federal court to preemptively block a Peltola victory in the upcoming election
Trump says that he personally told the Justice Department to file this suit
It is difficult to find an actual legal argument, much less a persuasive one, anywhere in the Trump DOJ’s complaint initiating the lawsuit

Trump’s lawsuit also runs afoul of something called the “ Purcell principle” — a concept that, ironically, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the same day that the Trump administration filed its suit — which says that federal courts should be reluctant to intervene in election-related disputes when the election itself is about to happen
It is likely, in other words, that the Trump administration’s attempt to overturn a Democratic victory that hasn’t even happened yet will fail
But the mere existence of this new lawsuit, which is known as United States v
Alaska , is an ominous sign that the Trump administration will use every tool in its shed to overturn Democratic victories in the upcoming election

So what are the actual legal arguments in the Alaska case? It is a bit of a stretch to even describe the Justice Department’s complaint in this case as a “legal” document, as the complaint does not so much as point to any law that either not-Senator Sullivan or the state of Alaska may have violated, and instead vaguely alludes to legal sources that use terms like “integrity.” Specifically, the Justice Department points to a federal law which says that it has four purposes, one of which is to “ protect the integrity of the electoral process .” It also points to the Supreme Court’s decision in Bullock v

Carter (1972), which said that “a State has an interest, if not a duty, to protect the integrity of its political processes from frivolous or fraudulent candidacies.” But the statute that Trump’s lawyers quote, the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 , does not concern which candidates’ names should appear on the ballot
As its name suggests, it is a law about voter registration, and it imposes requirements on states, such as requiring them to register voters when those voters obtain a driver’s license

Similarly, while Bullock does include a single line indicating that states may enact laws targeting “frivolous or fraudulent candidacies,” nothing in the opinion suggests that sharing another candidate’s name makes someone’s candidacy frivolous or fraudulent

The decision itself concerned unusually high fees charged to a candidate for public office in Texas, and the Court concluded that Texas’s fees were unconstitutional.  The line about “frivolous or fraudulent candidacies,” meanwhile, was included to clarify that states still have some power to regulate ballot access

While Bullock concluded that Texas’s fees were excessive, the opinion also suggests that states may impose more reasonable filing fees on candidates to discourage unserious candidates from seeking office
Alaska, for example, charges a modest filing fee of $100 to US Senate candidates

The Trump DOJ’s entire argument, in other words, appears to turn on the fact that it identified two legal sources that use the word “integrity” in contexts that bear little resemblance to the Alaska case.  Nevertheless, Trump’s lawyers claim that the court must prevent Alaska from certifying a Peltola victory “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J

Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.” This lawsuit also cannot be squared with one of the Republican Party’s favorite legal doctrines Even if Trump’s Justice Department had a persuasive argument that leaving not-Senator Sullivan on the ballot is illegal, they should still lose Alaska because they waited too long to file the case

Gonzalez (2006), the Supreme Court warned that “court orders affecting elections, especially conflicting orders, can themselves result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls,” and it added that this “risk will increase” as Election Day draws closer

More recent decisions, many of them joined only by the Court’s Republicans, have read this “ Purcell principle” quite expansively to forbid federal courts from issuing election-related decisions in the months leading up to an election
Justice Brett Kavanaugh has even claimed that Purcell prevents federal courts from issuing election-related decisions as soon as nine months before the general election date
Supreme Court decisions invoking Purcell to shut down lower court orders altering a state’s election rules are now very common in the weeks leading up to an election
On Thursday, for example, the Court relied on the Purcell principle to block a lower court order that would have made it easier for college students to vote in New Hampshire

The Court began its decision with this line: “This Court has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election.”  Trump’s DOJ, meanwhile, did not even file its lawsuit seeking to preemptively invalidate a Peltola victory until less than two weeks before Election Day
If Purcell means anything, it must mean that a federal court cannot force Alaska to kick a candidate off the ballot mere days before a federal election.

body: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on
Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely
Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please

Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really? In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades
From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download

So stay tuned! In the biotech world, you can’t see everything —Jessica Hamzelou Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled
But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects
The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything
The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative
This is why it left me questioning how we cover science
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter
