<title>Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear</title>
    <content type="html"><p>On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers <a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/commercials/1964/peace-little-girl-daisy">watched a little girl counting petals</a> on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.</p>

<p>The ad <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/sites/default/files/2023-09/Epstein_0.pdf">ran as a paid spot only once</a>, in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/44090431">opponent, republican Barry Goldwater</a>. The ad played on a fear voters already held, <a href="https://ropercenter.cornell.edu/blog/public-opinion-about-using-nuclear-weapons">that Goldwater might start a nuclear war</a>. Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-daisy-ad-changed-everything-about-political-advertising-180958741/">uproar got it rebroadcast</a> in full on network news.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/riDypP1KfOU?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Formally titled ‘Peace, Little Girl,’ this political commercial was produced for President Lyndon B. Johnson’s 1964 campaign against Barry Goldwater.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1041794X.2012.712194">reactions to political ads</a> to how <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2958.2006.00006.x">anxiety drives people to seek out</a>, and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.</p>

<p>The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day <a href="https://www.facebook.com/TCDearborn/posts/republican-us-senate-candidate-mike-rogers-new-ad-targeting-abdul-el-sayed-is-ra/1756483326329553/">continue to reach for fear</a>, and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.</p>

<h2>Why campaigns use fear</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.2016.16030353">Fear is an alarm</a>. It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.</p>

<p>Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.</p>

<p>When political scientists <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=X2Sg8SIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Travis Ridout</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=NIrlYoQAAAAJ&amp;hl">Kathleen Searles</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9221.2010.00819.x">tracked Senate ads</a> from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.</p>

<h2>Does fear change votes?</h2>

<p>Sometimes, fear works. </p>

<p>During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JPK--icAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Ted Brader</a> ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo3640346.html">changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical</a>. Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.</p>

<p>Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.</p>

<p>More broadly, a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0039729">meta-analysis of over 100 studies</a> found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=PPPSsQoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Lucy Popova</a> tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10410236.2013.824063">held less favorable attitudes</a> toward snus and were less inclined to try it.</p>

<p>Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2508.2007.00618.x">review of more than 100 studies</a> found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.</p>

<h2>The critical ingredient is empowerment</h2>

<p>Communication scholar <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=kxXEupgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Kim Witte’s</a> research found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03637759209376276">fear motivates action when</a> people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, <a href="https://theconversation.com/humans-are-hardwired-to-dismiss-facts-that-dont-fit-their-worldview-127168">people protect themselves from the message instead</a>. They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Graphic warnings on cigarette packages in Canada" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gruesome warnings on tobacco products can spark fear – but what’s the next step?</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/graphic-warnings-are-displayed-on-the-packaging-of-news-photo/2262538399">Creative Touch Imaging Ltd./NurPhoto via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.</p>

<p>My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2958.2006.00006.x">sought out the most information</a>. Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.</p>

<p>A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.</p>

<p>Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=1ed6QpkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">Nicholas Valentino</a> and colleagues found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381610000939">anger boosted voter participation</a> more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.</p>

<h2>Fear plays on prejudice and stereotypes</h2>

<p>Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.</p>

<p>One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/TKXx8GnOgA4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The ‘Revolving Door’ ad attacked Democratic presidential candidate Michael Dukakis’ record on crime.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Bush’s campaign followed up with the “<a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/commercials/1988/revolving-door">Revolving Door</a>” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes. </p>

<p>Political scientist <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=-OEfcQ8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Tali Mendelberg’s</a> research described in “<a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691070711/the-race-card">The Race Card</a>” shows that these implicit <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/wing-playbook-against-abdul-el-212947742.html">appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful</a>. But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.</p>

<p>Gender works in a similar way. </p>

<p>In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=IzWWT4EAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Mirya Holman</a> and colleagues found that when campaign <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1065912915624018">messages triggered fears of terrorism</a>, voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1065912915624018">tough on security</a>.</p>

<p>A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability <a href="https://theintercept.com/2026/07/27/abdul-el-sayed-haley-stevens-aipac-senate-michigan/">for Muslim candidates</a>.</p>

<h2>Is fear a more common tactic now?</h2>

<p><a href="https://emotionresearcher.com/the-use-and-consequences-of-emotions-in-politics/">Using fear as a campaign tool</a> is nothing new. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="black-and-white document 'Some account of the bloody deeds of General Andrew Jackson' with coffin illustrations" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=942&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=942&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=942&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1184&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1184&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1184&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Anti-Andrew Jackson handbills circulated around the 1828 presidential election.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Some_account_of_the_bloody_deeds_of_General_Andrew_Jackson,_circa_1828.png">University of Pittsburgh/Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate <a href="https://reagan.blogs.archives.gov/2022/10/31/american-elections-and-campaigns-1828-a-sign-of-things-to-come/">Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism</a>. Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “<a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/commercials/1984/bear">Bear</a>” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that <a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/websites/cg96/ad1024.htm">seniors’ Medicare was at risk</a>.</p>

<p>What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 <a href="https://www.press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/284996.html">documents that rise</a>, though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.</p>

<p>The current media landscape shifts this dynamic significantly; while traditional <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/fact-sheet/network-news/">nightly news broadcasts have seen a decline</a> in viewership, targeted social media feeds have become the emotional battleground.</p>

<p>Recent digital campaign data shows that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055420000696">negative ads are highly prized online</a> because they successfully grab attention by provoking strong emotions like fear and anger. Because platform recommendation systems are heavily <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-social-media-algorithms-send-you-posts-you-dont-like-288792">driven by user activity</a>, campaigns are incentivized to use emotionally charged appeals to maximize viral engagement across feeds.</p>

<p>Fear works less like a switch and more like a spotlight. It grabs attention and opens minds to change, but whether that turns into a vote, a boycott of the ballot box or resentment toward the messenger depends on what comes next.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292574/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Creative Touch Imaging Ltd./NurPhoto via Getty Images For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem
My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments
We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information
Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little
Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning
Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls

Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on

title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
excerpt: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
body: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores

But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it
Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture
There is only the right solution for the business problem
A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight
An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures
The constraints should determine the architecture
That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments
During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion

Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic
A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements
Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t
The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload
That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern
It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost
Engineer the system, not the model Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another
Serving architecture influences memory utilization
Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency
Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value
This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance
During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length
As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available
Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive
The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize
Then determine if another bottleneck emerged
Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all
The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements
For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question
Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value
Build for change, not today’s benchmark Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s
The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs
A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset
EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series
It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models
Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes

title: Making the case for context-aware AI
excerpt: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
body: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one
As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says
Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know
The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use
A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve
Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them
Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling
This approach could also change how employees spend their time
Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions
Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents
Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales
With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly

As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis

Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace
This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis
Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads
After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle
By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit
They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized
My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis
Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today

Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question
And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned
As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization
We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes
There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency
In either of them, we have some processes in place
You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first
Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task
And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate
And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context
And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise
And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come
To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making
If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic
Let’s just take the setting I was describing
